text: Good morning, everyone. Welcome to the July 18th meeting of the Economic Advisory Commission. We have a couple of items I wanted to bring to your attention.
As members of the Economic Advisory Commission, projects that in large measure you've either initiated or have been involved in over the past several months, first of all is the Talent Up Fund.

Many of you will recall that you met in a work session, and then we, as a full EAC, discussed that project. On July 11th, the Board of Supervisors approved the Talent Up Fund, which is a work-based learning opportunity fund.

The Talent Up will match local employers with qualified but untapped talent through paid temp-to-permanent work-based learning internships. Selling up as a pilot program utilizing $2.5 million of ARPA funding, federal funding.

The program will launch later this year and run through 2024. It is an initiative of the Economic Advisory Commission, and we thank you for your work and input. Last year, staff then developed a program based on that input, guidance, and your expertise.

Staff's going to communicate with the EAC when the employer engagement begins this fall. So the second program I wanted to mention was the Thrive Small Business Technical Assistance Program. This is an initiative of the Department of Economic Initiatives, and they would like you to know about the program because we need your input.

It's going to provide up to $10,000 in technical assistance to small businesses in areas including marketing, operations, and finance. It's currently recruiting experienced consultants to provide that technical assistance.

And there are RFPs that are now open through August 4th. So if you're interested or you know a consulting firm that might be able to offer its services to this program or you know a small business that would be in need of these technical services, please let us know.

You can reach out to Rebecca Modery and the Department of Economic Initiatives with that information. So the meeting we have today is focused on one of the biggest challenges we, I think, as a board, see going forward, and that is the preservation and expansion of our commercial office space.

Very fortunate to have some great speakers here today to help us understand the issues and discuss with you your suggestions and ideas on how we move forward in that arena. Our first presentation is going to be an overview by Rebecca Mildry, the director of the Department of Economic Initiatives, and Scott Sizer, who works in that department.

We'll then have a presentation on a current office market and leasing trends with the EDA and also the EDA will present an office vacancies and solutions presentation. And finally, Andy Dorlester from the Department of Planning and Development will present on building conversions.

And I want to point out that if Andy screws up, there's nothing we can do because she's leaving Fairfax County on Thursday. So, you know, so we're at her mercy. And she said something about getting it off her mind.

I'm not sure what that meant. Anyway, Andy, it's been fun working with you, and you've done a great job for the county over 24 years. So thank you for that, and good luck at your next endeavor. We had an excellent, I think, set of minutes from our last get-together that was distributed.

Did anyone have any changes or revisions to those minutes? If not, they'll stand as a record of our last EAC meeting. So with that, I think I will just turn it over to Rebecca Mowdry because we have a very busy agenda.

We do. I'm going to briefly introduce the topic and the agenda. But before I do, I'm going to do something that I don't get a chance too often, which is recognize someone who helps us put this entire meeting together, even picks up coffee so that we can all have a little networking beforehand, puts the slides up, creates the agenda.

So I just want to recognize my colleague, Mariam Clumley. Thank you very much, Mariam, for all of your help. Lots of behind-the-scenes work, of course. So again, I'm going to introduce the topic. and many would say that this conversation is a long time coming, but we really believe that today, right now, is the best time to discuss the office market. Since March of 2020, we have certainly been moving through some uncertain economic times, and in spite of that uncertainty,

or maybe because of that uncertainty, we have all responded and acted in creative and courageous ways and that has helped to continue a strong economy and workforce and we continue to see robust economic activity even now. We've seen many changes and perhaps one of the greatest changes that we've seen is changes in the workplace. How we work, where we work, when we work, why we work
And these questions and our response to it are crucial for us today and also for our tomorrow, especially given that in Fairfax County, we have 120 million square feet of office space.

So this discussion today and our ongoing activities certainly will have an impact on our economy and our workers. And we see a lot of news stories and data and analysis from different parts of our region and our nation on different office markets.

Many of those are ominous. Many are conflicting and certainly can create more uncertainty and perhaps more fear. So we are excited today to focus in on our unique office market in Fairfax County and review what's happening here and trends and also have a robust discussion about what we are doing and what we could be doing to continue to support our economy and ensure that businesses and workers want to come here, stay here, grow here.

Moving on, I went through the goals and some of the topics that we're going to go through. In terms of our agenda, Supervisor Faust presented the topics as well as our speakers. We have reserved a significant amount of time for discussion.

And what we'd like to do is kind of go through the presentations, present the information, close out with Andy, which feels appropriate as your swan song. and at the conclusion of Andy's presentation, open it up for questions and discussion as well as feedback. So with that, I'd like to turn it over to Scott Sizer. Thank you, Rebecca. As mentioned, I'm Scott Sizer with the Department of Economic Initiatives, and really one of the foundational documents and one of the big changes that happened since 2020 was the adoption of the countywide strategic plan by the board in 2021. This is really our shared vision of what the

community's goals and outcomes are in our county. It was adopted with 10 community outcome areas, These are the 10 issues of greatest importance to the community. And all of these are relevant and interrelated to the work of the EAC and economic development more broadly. But today, I wanted to focus on that economic opportunity outcome area, and the expressed vision that all businesses, people, and places are thriving economically.

So while it was adopted, really one of the big questions is, what's next? You know, how do we move from this goal to implementation? What does success look like? So that's where these five bullets on this slide start to speak to those desired outcomes of what this economic opportunity can look like for our community.

And it also includes a number of strategies that were proposed to meet these goals. The economic outcome section of the countywide strategic plan has 19 different strategies related to economic opportunity. And these, again, came out of work with the community as part of the strategic planning effort, as well as informed by the chairman's task force on equity and opportunity.

And so as the countywide plan moves into our second year of operation, the county executive has created an implementation team to make recommendations to move forward these 19 strategies, help to identify and prioritize those. And I think members of the EAC and members of the Board of Supervisor and staff will be helping with those efforts.

And today's discussion is really informing that work going forward. And it's really key for our discussion today, as Rebecca touched on, is the health and economic vibrancy of a subset of our economy, and that's really the office market. This dashboard that you see in front of you is currently up on the county's website.

And this is our key set of headline metrics for the economic opportunity section of the strategic plan. These are really used to help us identify those areas of performance and evaluate the goals and potential areas either for policy development, intervention. Again, this is currently up online.

These are really just those top headline measures. Behind these, there's additional data that's on the website that's shown below. Each one of these is really just the tip of the iceberg. As we'll see today, as we dive into the office market, there's just a tremendous amount of information and data and questions.

And every time you see a piece of information, sort of I've heard from folks as we were preparing for today, asking more questions and wanting to know more information about what's here. But today, really, we're going to be looking at that overall vacancy rate that's highlighted. But they're all linked and interrelate.

And I just want to show two quick graphs before we have our experts from the Fairfax County Economic Development Authority chime in. So this first graph is unemployment rate in Fairfax County. So what you're looking at here are monthly unemployment percentages dating back from 1990 all the way to 2022, the end of last year.

And so you can see a couple of different trends. The gray areas as well are areas, those are the months that the United States was in a national recession. And so you can start to see some patterns between recession impacts on unemployment rates. But I really just want to focus on that last end.

And as Rebecca mentioned, sort of the impact of the COVID-19 emergency and how unprecedented it was, this graph shows you that. I mean, it is, they were record high unemployment. It happened pretty immediately. There wasn't the buildup that you see in some of these other events.

It happened immediately, but then it has pretty quickly dropped back and returned to post-recession or post-COVID emergency or pre-COVID emergency numbers, including a recent report from the Northern Virginia Regional Commission has declared that we are back at pre-pandemic levels of unemployment going forward. And that's a very different graph than you'll see on the next one.

In this graph, I know when we look at it, there's just so much information and so much data here, and that's really the bulk of the discussion for today. This is illustrating our office market in Fairfax County from 1980 to December of 2022. So the past 42 years of our office market is represented in this one image. And so the yellow line is the direct vacancy rate. This is the amount of existing office square footage in those years that were vacant or unleased. A little bit of the darker line shows the sublet vacancy rates. So that also includes areas that are leased,

but the current tenant is seeking someone to either backfill or take space that they don't anticipate that they need. So that number is always going to be slightly higher than the yellow line. And then really important, to Rebecca's point, are those blue bars.

Those show the total office inventory that we have in the county. So in 1980, we had about 20 million square feet of office. And you could see the tremendous increase in growth to about 120 million square feet of office that we have today. So that's a tremendous amount of growth over those 40 years.

That means fundamental change in our office market as we went from a smaller, maybe more emerging office market to one of the largest, most diverse office markets in the nation. And so that really impacts those trend lines that we're seeing and how we're viewing those top line measures, but also our interventions and our policy strategies going forward.

And again, I would just point out, we saw in that previous slide, sort of that tremendous immediate impact of the COVID-19 emergency on the economic numbers. This graph looks very different. You've got basically since 2000, kind of an increase in vacancy rates for the last 20 years.

And so it's a very different trend and a fundamental trend and a long-term trend. And so I'm so happy that we have Victor Hoskins and Stephen Tardidi from the Economic Development Authority to really help us understand what's happening in our office market, how has that changed, and what does that mean going forward.
Thank you for that excellent introduction. And I guess we'll just go to the presentation by the Economic Development Authority, and then we'll take questions and comments. Mr. Victor Hoskins.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. My name is Victor Hoskins. I am the President and CEO of Fairfax County Economic Development. And I won't be reading these slides. I'd encourage you to read them. What I'm going to do is give you context for these slides. And this first one is really all about our mission.

We would not be able to achieve our mission without this board, without the executives in this room, the county executive and his team. There's no way 40 employees could do the kinds of things that we do unless we had partners like this incredible group here.

Whether it's Chairman McKay, you know, being on a show with Paraton, Talking about, you know, a virtual career fair we have or, you know, Supervisor Stork down at the National Building Museum, National Army Museum, recruiting, helping us recruit, you know, talent from the veterans.

Or Supervisor Gross helping us develop relationships with Fort Belvoir so that we can go down there every week and help these veterans in transition. Mike Batt has a team down there every week talking to these veterans, and he is a veteran, so he speaks their language. But we couldn't do these things without you.

And I will just say this. Last Friday, County Executive Hill and his team, the transportation team, working with VDOT, solved the problem for one of our biggest tenants, a 400,000-square-foot tenant that was not very happy with some of the things that were going on. So you help us with solutions.

You help us with talent and skill. You're involved in our work in ribbon cuttings like Supervisor Alcorn was with us at Cargo Sense, small company with a big global footprint. That kind of support, we couldn't win without it. These numbers prove it. 652,000 payroll jobs right now, highest number ever in the history of this county.

There was a report that just came out from Stephen Fuller Institute, which basically said, the center of growth for this region has moved. It's moved to Northern Virginia. Not only has it moved to Northern Virginia, but it's primarily here, here in Fairfax County. On a veteran side, I just want to mention, I have to mention this number because in the last two quarters, we work with these V3 companies.

These are Virginia Values Veteran companies. We have to certify these. We went from 700 last year to 1,400 this year. In the last two quarters, they have hired 3,800 veterans or spouses through our efforts.

And it's only because you funded those efforts. That's the only reason we can do it. And it just makes a huge difference in these numbers. The programs that you supported during the crisis, during the pandemic, Giving grants to these companies with 50 employees or less made a huge difference.

That 42,000 employee establishments, that number, the highest number was 36,000. It's 42,000 now. You have more employer establishments. That's people with payroll, with employees, because you created that bridge, you created a pivot, and now you've created a Thrive program.

And these have come out of DEI, the county executive's office, and they have made a huge difference. We have over 8,000 minority companies. This is all about our services. We deliver a lot of services. We meet with thousands of companies a year. Two-thirds of our job is to retain our clients, to keep the clients that are here, here.

We almost lost a major hotelier. It was an interesting competition, but because of the efforts of Supervisor Palachuk, the county executive, and others, we were able to retain them with help from the state of Virginia. But we do that only because you are our partners.

You make the difference. What I'd like to do is talk about some of these companies. These are some of the companies that have come to us recently. Great corporate citizens like StarKiss, they came here, they immediately started a food program of feeding families. You know, Hilton, incredible brand, went out of the Fortune 500, came back into the Fortune 500.

We have 10 Fortune 500 companies again, which is great. We have 113 Inc. 5000, fastest-growing companies in the country here in Fairfax. We are really – we're getting our share of business out there right now. And we have companies, of course, like Amazon working down in Supervisor Lusk area doing some interesting work.

But we also have these really focused on diversity. As you can see up there, we're number one on the eastern seaboard for diverse companies prospering. We have some incredible companies here, like Thompson. I know a lot of you know that this company started with only a few employees, now has thousands of employees.

I think their revenues last year were $825 million. They're targeting a billion for the next 24 months. You had the St. James. A lot of you guys have taken your kids to soccer games there. St. James just expanded into Reston. We have companies that believe in this community and are an integral part of this community and trust you and trust us.

Talent. Talent is a new currency of economic development. When I arrived here four years ago, you had funded a talent program, and we designed that program and implemented that program. And at this point, we can boast that we've had over 2,500 people connected directly to jobs through our digital hub.

We've had 1.5 million visitors there in the last three years. We started it right at COVID. We've had 10,000 in-person or virtual career interviews directly with recruiters, and we work with over 17,000 companies. On the academic side, we started out with 15 universities.

We now work with over 100 universities across the country, 40 of them at historically black colleges. We work with Women That Code and a number of other organizations. A big part of what we do is marketing. We've had a great year, actually the greatest year in the history of our county for earned media.

We get roughly a million dollars in media money from you every year. in 2020, we hit $36 million in earned media. This year, we hit $1.1 billion. I've only been able to do that one other time in my history of my career, and that was in Arlington County, and I had Amazon. So it's interesting to do it with smaller companies and really getting them into the Wall Street Journal. We had Appian in the Wall Street Journal twice. We've been in Fortune Japan. We do this globally, and we do this locally, but it's because of people like

Anna Nenissen and Andrew and the other people on our team that we're able to do this. And with that, I'm going to turn it over to Stephen Tardidi to talk about the office market. Thank you very much, supervisors and commissioners, for giving us the opportunity to give you a peek under the hood into our local office market. I think the conversation today will spark a lot of healthy discussion regarding the insights provided and possible actions taken. But before we can get into our local market, I think it's really important to put the vacancy rate issue into

context. And we want to do that by taking a look at this on a national level. This is Cushman and Wakefield's U.S. office market report. And these metro markets you see here with the accompanying vacancy rates, those are our peer competitors. Those are the regions that we compete with to attract and retain office-based companies.

As you can see, many of them, compared to the Northern Virginia, Washington, D.C. region, are not looking at as favorable. And in fact, a lot of them have crossed the 25% vacancy rate mark, you know, even since then, and show no signs of slowing.

So before I get into our local market, I think it's also important to understand that the office market is a lagging economic indicator. And what I mean by that is exemplified or illustrated here in this slide. We had ICF, a company that's now headquartered in Reston.

They decided to lease this space, this brand new trophy office space in 2019 before the pandemic hit. So I think an article comes out like this or the move out of this company comes out and it looks like it might be a pandemic-induced response, but this was a decision and this flight to quality is a trend that's been happening for a while. Now, what we need to reconcile with is the 300,000 square feet plus that they vacated in that 1980s inventory and what would possibly

be the new demand in that building. But speaking of the inventory, we have 120 million square feet. that makes us the second largest suburban office market in the US. So as Scott mentioned, not only are we a large office market, not only are we a diverse office market, but, you know, we're also a very mature office market. And, you know, another way to put the word mature is by our inventory, aging inventory. So close to half of our office inventory was built before 1990.

So there is going to need to be action on that inventory that has not kept up with the demand in the workforce expectations of today and tomorrow. And for that, and for examples like ICF that I mentioned, our vacancy rate is now at 16.7%. That's a direct office vacancy rate that recently crossed our previous 10-year high, which was as a result of sequestration. And so we just crossed that mark. I think there's still, I think the vacancy rate is going to climb a little bit more across the board on national level before it starts coming down. But I think where we,

when we're talking about relative to other markets and where we might have a competitive advantage is our diverse tenant base. Now, we have obviously our government contractors who, you know, a lot of that might be mission critical space in office use, and they're retaining that space. And you'll see that in a second. But in addition to that, in some of the companies that Victor was showing, we have corporate headquarters, which, you know, we count as an industry because they chose to be here for their stable business environment, and there's so many of them today.

We have 10 Fortune 500 companies headquartered here. We also have other office-based employers or employers that tend to use office space more, and that's in the construction and engineering, and some law firm presence as well, which a lot of them, they tell us when we talk to them that they didn't leave their office space even, you know, two days after the pandemic or got their employees back in. So they're able to build in that habit. So what we're hearing and seeing as far as it pertains to office leasing

and demand, our demand, the demand side of that is picking back up. Last year, we had 6.6 million square feet of office space leased. So we're at 37% below our pre-pandemic average. And comparing that to 2021, we were about 4.5 million square feet. So we continue to see these companies not only retain their space, but we're seeing new space added on there as well. Problem is we're seeing a bifurcation of the market, right? The class B, class C inventory, that's not seeing your net new tenant demand. It's your trophy office buildings. In fact, the trophy office

vacancy rate for Fairfax County is right around 10%, which is very healthy. So it's about solving for that the older inventory while taking a look away at catalyzing the new inventory and as I mentioned before the larger tenants are staying in place in the next slide I have some more information that really strongly reflects that point and then another another way that we're seeing the vacancy build up is the mid-sized tenants your 50,000 square foot tenants who might be in a class B building and they've decided I can cut my footprint in half take

25,000 square feet in a new office product, and I'll still pay the same paycheck to the landlord. The good news here, or the silver lining, is demand can be so volatile, so you can cut back on space. But if you're bringing your employees back in and they're demanding individual workplaces, you're going to have to build back that space up. Another strong sector of the market that we're seeing demand is co-working space. We've actually had two new co-working operators open in the past couple months, and we really stayed steady in that market, showing the small office businesses

increasing in that demand. There's actually a report from publication Coworking Cafe, and they ranked the top suburban office markets for coworking, and Washington, D.C. was number two behind L.A. So we have those options, and I think more and more building operators, if there is vacant space in newer buildings, they're looking to incorporate coworking space and have them graduate in that space.

You know, they grow a little bit longer. Okay, now we can lock you into a longer lease term. And across the board, from every brokerage firm we're talking to, tour activity is up, which is your first leading indicator of a space being leased. And I think it was 11% quarter over quarter, according to Lincoln Property Company.

So as I mentioned, when we're looking at our top tenants, our largest tenants and top deals for 2022, there's a couple stories here. The first one is we really know where our wheelhouse is, and that's in those government contractors.

You can see these deals are broken out into renewal, renewal contraction, or renewal growth, and then net new space. You can see only one company, when given the decision when their lease was expiring, decided to contract their space.

The rest of them either retained their space when they had that decision that they could cut out footprint. they've added more. Or, you know, we had one company that, or two companies that took new space. And that leads me into the other side of this story. The top two deals you see there are not government contractors. So, we continue to diversify our tenant base, while also recognizing that this is becoming a more and more competitive market every day for retention. We definitely recognize that the demand pie across the U.S. is smaller, so that makes retention very important.

And you see that second deal, the hospitality company that Victor mentioned, that was a competitive retention deal. So a lot of that, you know, we talk about the net new demand coming in, but we also need to make sure that the companies that are here are happy and looking to grow.

And then, so, you know, we were focusing on the larger companies. Now I'm going to go on to some of the smaller businesses and where we're seeing good leading indicators for future office demand. And remember what I said in the beginning, the office market is a lagging economic indicator.

But for these, all record highs that we're seeing could eventually lead to office space or already have. So record number of businesses. We have over 42,000 employer businesses. Victor mentioned this before, companies with payroll. One of the largest industry sectors that we saw a jump in those employer businesses was computer systems and design. So that's good, and that shows that there would be future office demand as a new company is established. The money is in flowing.

Typically, we would see around $500 million in venture capital come into Fairfax County-based companies. Last year, we had over a billion, and we're expecting across that number as well. I think the latest is we're already at $800 million. And then the record labor force and employees that Victor was mentioning before. So you have your companies, they're getting the funding, and we have the workforce to support them. We think this is a good leading indicator for future office demand for homegrown businesses. But now looking at the national context again and seeing where

we're hearing about either economic indicators or stories about economic trends and how they might impact our market we broke that out into low impact medium impact and high impact uh you know we've been through several recession cycles before here in fairfax county with a similar market and both times um especially relative uh to the national level we've come out on top this time around i think it's uh really because of the um you know the industry mix that we have you know you look at these other markets where they either had uh mass layoff events or they're putting large

blocks of space on the market. And those are centralized in a lot of your consumer tech. So we're fortunate to have more of that, either business to government or business to business tech. And so we haven't really seen major light off events in Fairfax County. Where we could see some impact coming is obviously in office activity. And I think what I'd want to stress with this is that the dust is very much not settled on this. I think, you know, we're looking, we hear a different story about RTO and where, where it's going. But recently in the past couple of months, we're seeing, especially for Fairfax County companies, we're seeing the biggest push to get

their employees back into the office. Um, and you know, I think the, it's a double-edged sword because the other side of that is we have such a high concentration of office using industries. So that can, you know, you're talking about a large market and the industries that will call back their employees and have them come in and somehow push back and what that will mean for vacant space in the future. Interest rates would really see that impact on the inventory side, not necessarily the leasing side for our market. Other markets, because of what interest rates

have done, companies have paused their either expansion plans or their decisions or have gone through those mass levels that I was talking about before. But on the product side is where we're seeing that when these building owners, you know, going into refinancing at the current interest rates, it really poses a problem for how office buildings are valued. And that is still very much a bit in the air, but we're starting to see that come on the horizon. Some of the high impact areas, listen, we're in a tight labor market. We really are. I think last year we had

across the U.S. we had two open jobs for every worker. Now I think that number is more around 1.5. But if you have a high office base of employment and you have a very tight labor market, there's more chance or opportunity for volatility there. Someone saying, well, I can go to this company, I can go here. And especially if there is more of that hybrid work or remote work, they, you know, they could choose to lose the area, and we are, but we're such a strong market for talent. We want to make sure we're monitoring that, and we continue to keep those employees here. I think at the end of the day, we're already seeing this. Employees are

saying, you at least need to be tied to the office. You know, if, at the very least, if I call you into the office, you need to, it shouldn't be a four-hour flight, right, or a different time zone. You have to sit here, so. And then, of course, going to the office market vacancy, which we were talking about. I mean, the fact of the matter is, we are a large office market, and so it's, you know, as far as tracking when employers are leaving or going to the space and making sure they're staying here, you know, there is a bit of a spinning plate effect just because we have such a robust inventory. There's more opportunities for that vacancy to come online.

So, I was focusing more on the demand side. Now, I'll go into our inventory. there was, when we're looking at both our inventory and our vacancy, there's a couple ways to cross cut that. Inventory, like I said before, almost half of our office inventory was built before 1990. So if you think about what type of building that was, that was typically a three building suburban office campus on top of surface parking lot with not a lot of walkable amenities and not really, you know, aside from some employers and office-based industries,

not really tuned to the workforce of today and tomorrow of what they're looking for. And then in the beginning of the 21st century is when we saw another jump. And, you know, that building, those buildings are still, what I'd say, is have good bones, but needs the placemaking or sense of place built around it, woven through it.

And there is one area in particular, say it's south of the toll road, where we're starting to see that. Much of that inventory was built 2000 to 2010. If you're familiar with the Woodland Park area, Dulles Corner, now you're starting to see residential and retail woven within that, and that will really make that an attractive neighborhood.

Now, when we're looking at the vacancy rate, we'll start at the highest level here, and we really broke this out into what is vacant office space that will either be released or a building might go through renovation, and then what's a vacant office space that is planned for redevelopment?

I mean, someone came in, they either acquired an office building or held it for a while and had plans to demolish that office building. Well, that number is close to 6 million square feet. So if you were to take 6 million square feet of inventory off the market, you would actually have the impact of reducing the vacancy rate to around 13%.

The problem is those projects aren't moving forward right now for various ways. A lot of that is the underlying market and finances behind the project. but it's in the can, right? It's planned for, and especially where the market's going right now, we see eventually they'll be replaced. You can also take a look, in addition to what will be held for redevelopment or adaptive reuse, the various different types of office product and how the market solves for them or comes in. The new product is pretty obvious. That's really coming

online in those high demand areas um you know they usually have options for for transit they usually have amenities surrounding and um and typically the between the the work that the the brokerages do and also what we do with our our talent team and filling the talent in there that product solves for itself uh and then we look into sort of the second generation that's your established or a commodity space. A lot of times where we see this inventory and when it turns over is it's client serving. This might be that more mission critical space that's in Chantilly that

might be vacant for half a year and might be a little bit older, but it's imperative to be close to that three-letter agency. And then renovation. This is when the landlord needs to decide whether they're going to infuse that capital and make that decision to get that building up to speed or to what the demands of the employers in the workforce is. Then, you know, we look at the product level and we'll go on to the space level here. I think this is, you know, I mentioned the diverse office product as one of the competitive advantages. We actually recently

had a company that was new to market and they were in a market that only or primarily only had high rise office buildings. But for their operations, they had deliveries coming in and they really need to be in a one-story office building. We were fortunate enough that we could offer that opportunity and provide that space for them in the future. And then also for future growth, you know, we have similar product like that. So I do think you, you know, while too much vacancy obviously is not good, you do want a certain level of vacant office space and a diverse

office product for those companies that can come and be attracted to our accounting. We can also look at where the location of the large blocks or vacant spaces and how much of it is. I'd say about 70% of our large block spaces reside in what we constitute as the dullest toll road submarkets. The good news here is a lot of that inventory was built out in the 1980s and will be part of that held for redevelopment and slated for demolition.
